interleave.title: How interleave() works
interleave.description: Takes turns between two iterators until both are empty.

note.text: takes turns: one from each, until both are empty

slides.caption: interleave() gets two iterators: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (from 1..7) and -1, -2.
It takes one item from each in turn: 1, then -1, then 2, then -2.
The second iterator has run out. interleave() keeps going with the first one until it is empty too: 3, 4, 5, 6.

dedup.title: How dedup() works
dedup.description: Removes repeated items that sit next to each other.

note.text: removes repeats that sit right next to each other

slides.caption: dedup() gets the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2.
Each item is compared with the item just before it. A second 1, a second 3 and a second 2 are equal to their neighbour, so they are repeats (red).
The 2 at position 5 stays: the item before it is 3, not 2. Only neighbours are compared, not the whole sequence.
Repeats are dropped; the first item of every run is kept, in order.
dedup() yields 1, 2, 3, 2

chunks.title: How chunks() works
chunks.description: Hands out the items in groups of n; the last group may be shorter.

slides.caption: chunks(3) reads the items 1 to 7 and hands them out in groups of 3.
The first 3 items form the first group: [1, 2, 3].
The next 3 items form the second group: [4, 5, 6].
Only 7 is left, so the last group is shorter: [7]. Nothing is dropped and nothing is padded.
(1..=7).chunks(3) gives the groups [1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6] and [7]. Each group is an iterator of its own; collect it to get a Vec.

tuple-windows.title: How tuple_windows() works
tuple-windows.description: Gives every pair of neighbours; the pairs overlap.

note.text: a window of 2 that moves one step at a time

slides.caption: tuple_windows() looks at the items through a window as wide as the tuple type, here 2.
The window starts on the first two items and yields (1, 2).
It moves one step to the right: (2, 3). The 2 is used again.
One more step: (3, 4). The window has reached the end.
Four items give three overlapping pairs: (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4). Use tuples() for pairs that do not overlap.

circular-tuple-windows.title: How circular_tuple_windows() works
circular-tuple-windows.description: Like tuple_windows(), but the window wraps around to the start.

note.text: the last window wraps around to the first item

slides.caption: circular_tuple_windows() treats the items as if they were in a circle: after 3 comes 1 again.
The first window is (1, 2).
Then (2, 3), as with tuple_windows().
The window now starts at the last item. There is nothing after 3, so it wraps around and takes 1: (3, 1).
Three items give three windows, one starting at each item: (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1).

tuples.title: How tuples() works
tuples.description: Groups items into tuples that do not overlap; leftovers are not yielded.

slides.caption: tuples() fills one tuple at a time; the tuple type (_, _) says each tuple has 2 items.
The first two items make (1, 2).
The next two make (3, 4). Unlike tuple_windows(), no item is used twice.
5 is left, but a pair needs two items. tuples() does not yield an incomplete tuple, so 5 is not part of the result.
The result is (1, 2), (3, 4). The leftover 5 can still be read with .into_buffer() on the Tuples iterator.

unique.title: How unique() works
unique.description: Removes every repeated item and keeps the first time each one appears.

note.text: remembers every item it has seen

slides.caption: unique() keeps a set of the items it has already yielded.
3 has not been seen: it is yielded and remembered.
1 is new too: yielded.
3 is already in the set, so it is skipped, even though it is not next to the first 3.
2 is new: yielded.
1 was seen before: skipped.
unique() yields 3, 1, 2: first-seen order is kept. Compare dedup(), which only removes repeats that are neighbours.

unique-by.title: How unique_by() works
unique-by.description: Keeps the first item for each key a function computes.

slides.caption: unique_by() remembers keys, not items. The key here is the first letter of each word.
"apple" has key 'a', which is new: "apple" is yielded.
"avocado" also has key 'a'. The word is different, but the key was seen, so it is skipped.
"berry" has key 'b', which is new: yielded.
The result is "apple", "berry": one word for each first letter, the first one found.

dedup-with-count.title: How dedup_with_count() works
dedup-with-count.description: Collapses each run of equal neighbours into (count, item).

slides.caption: dedup_with_count() walks the items and counts how long each run of equal neighbours is.
Two 'a's in a row: one run of length 2, yielded as (2, 'a').
'b' is different, so a new run starts. It has length 1: (1, 'b').
Another 'a'. It is not next to the first run, so it is a new run: (1, 'a').
The count comes first in each tuple. Use counts() for a total per item instead: 'a' would be 3.

counts.title: How counts() works
counts.description: Counts how many times each item appears, in a HashMap.

note.text: a frequency table: item → number of times

slides.caption: counts() reads every item and adds 1 to that item's counter in a HashMap.
'h' gets a counter: 1.
'e' gets a counter: 1.
'l' gets a counter: 1.
'l' again: its counter goes up to 2. The two l's did not have to be neighbours.
'o' gets a counter: 1.
The result is a HashMap<char, usize>. A HashMap has no fixed order; the counts are shown here in the order the letters first appear.

into-group-map.title: How into_group_map() works
into-group-map.description: Collects (key, value) pairs into a HashMap of key → list of values.

note.text: one list of values per key

slides.caption: into_group_map() reads pairs. The first part is the key, the second is a value to add to that key's list.
Key "a" is new: it gets the list [1].
Key "b" is new: it gets the list [2].
Key "a" already has a list, so 3 is pushed onto it: [1, 3]. Values keep their input order.
The result is a HashMap<&str, Vec<i32>>. The map itself has no fixed order (keys are sorted here); each list is in input order.

cartesian-product.title: How cartesian_product() works
cartesian-product.description: Pairs every item of one iterator with every item of another.

slides.caption: cartesian_product() takes each item of the first iterator and pairs it with every item of the second.
1 is paired with 'a' and then with 'b'.
Then 2 is paired with 'a' and with 'b'. The second iterator is cloned so it can be walked again.
The first item changes slowest, like the outer loop of two nested for loops.

eq.text: for x in 1..=2 { for y in [a, b] { (x, y) } }

slides.caption: 2 items × 2 items give 4 pairs: (1, 'a'), (1, 'b'), (2, 'a'), (2, 'b').

multi-cartesian-product.title: How multi_cartesian_product() works
multi-cartesian-product.description: Every combination that takes one item from each of many lists.

note.text: one item from each list, in every possible way

slides.caption: multi_cartesian_product() works on an iterator of lists. Each result is a Vec with one item from every list.
Take 0 from list 1 and 0 from list 2: [0, 0].
The last list advances first: [0, 1].
List 2 is used up, so list 1 advances and list 2 starts again: [1, 0].
Then [1, 1]. Both lists are used up, so the iterator ends.
With n lists this is like n nested loops: these are the binary numbers 00, 01, 10, 11.

combinations.title: How combinations() works
combinations.description: Every way to choose k items, when order does not matter.

note.text: choose 2 of 3; [2, 1] is the same choice as [1, 2]

slides.caption: combinations(2) yields every way to choose 2 of the items, keeping them in their original order.
Start with the first two items: [1, 2].
Keep 1 and move the second choice on: [1, 3].
Move the first choice on to 2. Only 3 can follow it: [2, 3].
Choices like [2, 1] or [3, 1] are never made: they hold the same items as [1, 2] and [1, 3].
The result is [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3]. permutations(2) would also give the reversed orders: 6 in all.

combinations-with-replacement.title: How combinations_with_replacement() works
combinations-with-replacement.description: Like combinations(), but an item may be chosen more than once.

note.text: choose 2, and the same item may be picked again

slides.caption: combinations_with_replacement(2) puts each chosen item back, so it can be chosen again.
1 is chosen, put back, and chosen again: [1, 1].
Then 1 and 2: [1, 2].
2 twice: [2, 2]. [2, 1] is not given: it is the same choice as [1, 2].
Plain combinations(2) of [1, 2] would only give [1, 2]. With replacement there are 3 choices.

permutations.title: How permutations() works
permutations.description: Every ordered arrangement of k items: order matters.

slides.caption: permutations(2) yields every way to arrange 2 of the 3 items in a row.
1 first, then each of the others: [1, 2], [1, 3].
2 first: [2, 1], [2, 3]. [2, 1] counts, because the order is different from [1, 2].
3 choices for the first place × 2 for the second = 6. combinations(2) gives only 3.
All 6 arrangements, in order of the first item.

powerset.title: How powerset() works
powerset.description: Every subset of the items, from the empty one to all of them.

slides.caption: powerset() yields all combinations of size 0, then size 1, then size 2, and so on.
Size 0: the empty subset [].
Size 1: each item on its own.
Size 2: the combinations of 2 items.
Size 3: all the items. Each item is either in or out of a subset, so there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 subsets.
All 8 subsets. The number doubles with every extra item, so long inputs give huge results.

join.title: How join() works
join.description: Turns the items into one String with a separator between them.

note.text: the separator goes between items, not after the last

slides.caption: join() formats every item with Display and glues them into one String.
The first item starts the string: "1".
Before each later item, the separator ", " is added: "1, 2".
Then ", 3". There are no more items, so nothing is added after the 3.
join(", ") returns the String "1, 2, 3". An empty iterator gives an empty String.

intersperse.title: How intersperse() works
intersperse.description: Puts a separator item between every two items.

note.text: a 0 between items, never at the ends

slides.caption: intersperse(0) yields the items as they are, with a 0 between each pair of neighbours.
The first item, 1, comes out unchanged.
Before the next item a 0 is yielded, then 2.
Another 0, then 3.
The input is empty, so intersperse() stops. There is no 0 after the last item.
intersperse(0) yields 1, 0, 2, 0, 3. Use join() when you want a String instead.

merge.title: How merge() works
merge.description: Merges two sorted iterators into one sorted iterator.

note.text: both inputs are sorted, so the output is sorted too

slides.caption: merge() only ever looks at the front item of each input and yields the smaller one.
Compare the fronts: 1 and 2. 1 is smaller, so it comes out first.
Now 4 and 2: 2 is smaller.
4 and 3: 3 is smaller.
The first list is empty, so the rest of the second follows: 8.
Each item is compared once or twice, no sorting needed. If the inputs are not sorted, the output is not sorted either.

kmerge.title: How kmerge() works
kmerge.description: Merges any number of sorted iterators into one sorted iterator.

note.text: the smallest front item comes out each time

slides.caption: kmerge() keeps the front item of every list in a small heap and always yields the smallest.
Fronts: 1, 2, 3. The smallest is 1.
Fronts: 4, 2, 3. The smallest is 2.
Fronts: 4, 5, 3. The smallest is 3.
Fronts: 4, 5, 6. 4 comes out.
Then 5.
Only 6 is left.
Three sorted lists merged into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. With two lists, merge() does the same.

zip-longest.title: How zip_longest() works
zip-longest.description: Walks two iterators side by side and keeps going until both are empty.

slides.caption: zip_longest() yields an EitherOrBoth for each position: Both when both sides have an item, Left or Right when only one does.
Both sides have an item: Both(1, 'a').
The right side is empty. zip() would stop here; zip_longest() yields Left(2).
And Left(3). Then both sides are empty and it stops.
Every item appears once. Match on Both, Left and Right to handle each case.

interleave-shortest.title: How interleave_shortest() works
interleave-shortest.description: Takes turns between two iterators and stops when the one whose turn it is runs out.

note.text: stops as soon as a turn cannot be taken

slides.caption: interleave_shortest() takes one item from each side in turn, starting with the first.
First side: 1.
Second side: 2.
First side: 3. Second side: 4.
First side: 5.
It is the second side's turn, but it is empty, so the iterator stops. 7 is never yielded; interleave() would have yielded it.
The result is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Use interleave() to keep the rest of the longer side.

minmax.title: How minmax() works
minmax.description: Finds the smallest and the largest item in one pass.

note.text: both ends in one pass over the items

slides.caption: minmax() walks the items once and updates the smallest and largest seen so far.
The first item is both the smallest and the largest so far.
9 is larger than 4: the largest is now 9.
1 is smaller than 4: the smallest is now 1.
The items are used up. Calling min() and then max() would walk them twice.
The result is MinMax(1, 9). An empty iterator gives NoElements and a single item gives OneElement(x).

position-max.title: How position_max() works
position-max.description: Gives the index of the largest item, not the item itself.

slides.caption: position_max() remembers the largest item seen so far and its index.
Index 0 holds 4: the largest so far.
Index 1 holds 9, which is larger: remember index 1.
Index 2 holds 1, which is smaller: nothing changes.
The answer is the index, 1, wrapped in Some. When several items are equally large, the index of the last one is returned.
position_max() returns Some(1); an empty iterator gives None. max() would return Some(9) instead.

positions.title: How positions() works
positions.description: Gives the index of every item that matches a condition.

slides.caption: positions() tests every item and yields its index when the test is true.
Index 0 holds 1: odd, skipped.
Index 1 holds 2: even, so the index 1 is yielded.
Index 2 holds 3: odd, skipped.
Index 3 holds 4: even, so 3 is yielded.
The result is the indices 1, 3, not the items 2 and 4. Iterator::position() only finds the first match.

k-smallest.title: How k_smallest() works
k-smallest.description: Finds the k smallest items without sorting all of them.

note.text: only 2 items are kept at any time

slides.caption: k_smallest(2) keeps the 2 smallest items seen so far in a small heap. Anything larger is thrown away.
5 and 1 fill the 2 places.
4 is smaller than the largest kept item, 5, so 4 replaces 5.
2 is smaller than 4, so 2 replaces 4.
3 is larger than 2: it cannot be among the 2 smallest, so it is dropped.
At the end the kept items are sorted and yielded.
k_smallest(2) yields 1, 2. Memory use stays at k items, however long the input is.

sorted.title: How sorted() works
sorted.description: Collects any iterator and yields its items in sorted order.

slides.caption: sorted() cannot yield anything before it has seen every item: the smallest might be the last one.
First it collects all items into a Vec.
It sorts the Vec. 1 is smallest, so it comes out first.
Then 2.
Then 3.
sorted() yields 1, 2, 3 as an iterator, so you can keep chaining. The sort is stable: equal items keep their order.

sorted-by-key.title: How sorted_by_key() works
sorted-by-key.description: Sorts items by a key a function computes.

slides.caption: sorted_by_key() computes a key for every item and sorts by the keys.
The keys are the lengths: kiwi → 4, fig → 3, banana → 6.
The smallest key is 3: "fig" comes first.
Then key 4: "kiwi".
Then key 6: "banana".
Alphabetically the order would be banana, fig, kiwi. Items with equal keys keep their input order.

partition-map.title: How partition_map() works
partition-map.description: Splits items into two collections that can have different types.

note.text: Ok values go left, Err values go right

slides.caption: partition_map() calls a closure on each item. The closure returns Either::Left(v) or Either::Right(v), here: Ok(v) → Left(v), Err(e) → Right(e).
Ok(1) → Left(1): 1 goes into the left Vec<i32>.
Err("x") → Right("x"): "x" goes into the right Vec<&str>.
Ok(2) → Left(2).
The result is a tuple of two collections: ([1, 2], ["x"]). Iterator::partition() can only split into two collections of the same type.

coalesce.title: How coalesce() works
coalesce.description: Merges neighbouring items while a rule allows it.

note.text: merge (a, b) and (c, d) when c = b + 1

slides.caption: Each number becomes a range (x, x). coalesce() looks at the current range and the next one. The closure returns Ok(merged) to merge them, or Err to keep both.
The first range is (1, 1).
2 follows 1: merge into (1, 2).
3 follows 2: merge into (1, 3).
7 does not follow 3: (1, 3) is finished and yielded. (7, 7) starts.
8 follows 7: merge into (7, 8). The input ends, so (7, 8) is yielded.
Runs of consecutive numbers became ranges: (1, 3), (7, 8). The closure was |a, b| if a.1 + 1 == b.0 { Ok((a.0, b.1)) } else { Err((a, b)) }.

fold-while.title: How fold_while() works
fold-while.description: A fold that can stop before the end.

slides.caption: fold_while() works like fold(), but the closure returns Continue(acc) to go on or Done(acc) to stop. The closure: if acc + x <= 10 { Continue(acc + x) } else { Done(acc) }.
Start with acc = 0. 0 + 3 = 3 is ≤ 10: Continue(3).
3 + 4 = 7 is ≤ 10: Continue(7).
7 + 5 = 12 would be more than 10: Done(7). The fold stops here.
6 is never looked at.
fold_while() returns FoldWhile::Done(7); .into_inner() gives 7. A plain fold() cannot stop early.

all-equal.title: How all_equal() works
all-equal.description: Checks whether every item is equal to the first one.

note.text: compare every item with the first

slides.caption: all_equal() takes the first item and compares every other item with it. It stops at the first difference.
[2, 2, 2]: every item equals the first, so the answer is true.
[2, 3]: 3 differs from 2, so the answer is false.
An empty iterator has no items that differ, so it gives true. A single item gives true as well.
Watch out for the empty case: all_equal() is true when there is nothing to compare. Use all_equal_value() to get the value too.

exactly-one.title: How exactly_one() works
exactly-one.description: Gets the only item, or an error when there are zero or several.

note.text: Ok only when there is exactly one item

slides.caption: exactly_one() reads at most two items: one to return and one more to check that there is nothing else.
[5]: one item and then the end: Ok(5).
An empty iterator: there is no item to return: Err.
[1, 2]: a second item exists: Err. The error still holds 1 and 2, so nothing is lost.
Use exactly_one() when more or fewer items would be a bug, for example a lookup that must match one row.

interleave.title: How interleave() works
interleave.description: Takes turns between two iterators until both are empty.

note.text: takes turns: one from each, until both are empty

slides.caption: interleave() gets two iterators: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (from 1..7) and -1, -2.
It takes one item from each in turn: 1, then -1, then 2, then -2.
The second iterator has run out. interleave() keeps going with the first one until it is empty too: 3, 4, 5, 6.

dedup.title: How dedup() works
dedup.description: Removes repeated items that sit next to each other.

note.text: removes repeats that sit right next to each other

slides.caption: dedup() gets the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2.
Each item is compared with the item just before it. A second 1, a second 3 and a second 2 are equal to their neighbour, so they are repeats (red).
The 2 at position 5 stays: the item before it is 3, not 2. Only neighbours are compared, not the whole sequence.
Repeats are dropped; the first item of every run is kept, in order.
dedup() yields 1, 2, 3, 2

chunks.title: How chunks() works
chunks.description: Hands out the items in groups of n; the last group may be shorter.

slides.caption: chunks(3) reads the items 1 to 7 and hands them out in groups of 3.
The first 3 items form the first group: [1, 2, 3].
The next 3 items form the second group: [4, 5, 6].
Only 7 is left, so the last group is shorter: [7]. Nothing is dropped and nothing is padded.
(1..=7).chunks(3) gives the groups [1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6] and [7]. Each group is an iterator of its own; collect it to get a Vec.

tuple-windows.title: How tuple_windows() works
tuple-windows.description: Gives every pair of neighbours; the pairs overlap.

note.text: a window of 2 that moves one step at a time

slides.caption: tuple_windows() looks at the items through a window as wide as the tuple type, here 2.
The window starts on the first two items and yields (1, 2).
It moves one step to the right: (2, 3). The 2 is used again.
One more step: (3, 4). The window has reached the end.
Four items give three overlapping pairs: (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4). Use tuples() for pairs that do not overlap.

circular-tuple-windows.title: How circular_tuple_windows() works
circular-tuple-windows.description: Like tuple_windows(), but the window wraps around to the start.

note.text: the last window wraps around to the first item

slides.caption: circular_tuple_windows() treats the items as if they were in a circle: after 3 comes 1 again.
The first window is (1, 2).
Then (2, 3), as with tuple_windows().
The window now starts at the last item. There is nothing after 3, so it wraps around and takes 1: (3, 1).
Three items give three windows, one starting at each item: (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1).

tuples.title: How tuples() works
tuples.description: Groups items into tuples that do not overlap; leftovers are not yielded.

slides.caption: tuples() fills one tuple at a time; the tuple type (_, _) says each tuple has 2 items.
The first two items make (1, 2).
The next two make (3, 4). Unlike tuple_windows(), no item is used twice.
5 is left, but a pair needs two items. tuples() does not yield an incomplete tuple, so 5 is not part of the result.
The result is (1, 2), (3, 4). The leftover 5 can still be read with .into_buffer() on the Tuples iterator.

chunk-by.title: How chunk_by() works
chunk-by.description: Groups neighbouring items that have the same key.

note.text: neighbours with the same key share a group

slides.caption: chunk_by() computes a key for every item (here the item itself) and starts a new group each time the key changes.
The first two items both have key 1, so they form one group: [1, 1].
The key changes to 2: the first group ends and a new one starts: [2].
The key changes to 3. Both 3s sit next to each other, so they share the last group: [3, 3].
Only neighbours are grouped: [1, 2, 1] would give three groups. Before itertools 0.13 this method was called group_by.

unique.title: How unique() works
unique.description: Removes every repeated item and keeps the first time each one appears.

note.text: remembers every item it has seen

slides.caption: unique() keeps a set of the items it has already yielded.
3 has not been seen: it is yielded and remembered.
1 is new too: yielded.
3 is already in the set, so it is skipped, even though it is not next to the first 3.
2 is new: yielded.
1 was seen before: skipped.
unique() yields 3, 1, 2: first-seen order is kept. Compare dedup(), which only removes repeats that are neighbours.

unique-by.title: How unique_by() works
unique-by.description: Keeps the first item for each key a function computes.

slides.caption: unique_by() remembers keys, not items. The key here is the first letter of each word.
"apple" has key 'a', which is new: "apple" is yielded.
"avocado" also has key 'a'. The word is different, but the key was seen, so it is skipped.
"berry" has key 'b', which is new: yielded.
The result is "apple", "berry": one word for each first letter, the first one found.

dedup-with-count.title: How dedup_with_count() works
dedup-with-count.description: Collapses each run of equal neighbours into (count, item).

slides.caption: dedup_with_count() walks the items and counts how long each run of equal neighbours is.
Two 'a's in a row: one run of length 2, yielded as (2, 'a').
'b' is different, so a new run starts. It has length 1: (1, 'b').
Another 'a'. It is not next to the first run, so it is a new run: (1, 'a').
The count comes first in each tuple. Use counts() for a total per item instead: 'a' would be 3.

counts.title: How counts() works
counts.description: Counts how many times each item appears, in a HashMap.

note.text: a frequency table: item → number of times

slides.caption: counts() reads every item and adds 1 to that item's counter in a HashMap.
'h' gets a counter: 1.
'e' gets a counter: 1.
'l' gets a counter: 1.
'l' again: its counter goes up to 2. The two l's did not have to be neighbours.
'o' gets a counter: 1.
The result is a HashMap<char, usize>. A HashMap has no fixed order; the counts are shown here in the order the letters first appear.

into-group-map.title: How into_group_map() works
into-group-map.description: Collects (key, value) pairs into a HashMap of key → list of values.

note.text: one list of values per key

slides.caption: into_group_map() reads pairs. The first part is the key, the second is a value to add to that key's list.
Key "a" is new: it gets the list [1].
Key "b" is new: it gets the list [2].
Key "a" already has a list, so 3 is pushed onto it: [1, 3]. Values keep their input order.
The result is a HashMap<&str, Vec<i32>>. The map itself has no fixed order (keys are sorted here); each list is in input order.

cartesian-product.title: How cartesian_product() works
cartesian-product.description: Pairs every item of one iterator with every item of another.

slides.caption: cartesian_product() takes each item of the first iterator and pairs it with every item of the second.
1 is paired with 'a' and then with 'b'.
Then 2 is paired with 'a' and with 'b'. The second iterator is cloned so it can be walked again.
The first item changes slowest, like the outer loop of two nested for loops.

eq.text: for x in 1..=2 { for y in [a, b] { (x, y) } }

slides.caption: 2 items × 2 items give 4 pairs: (1, 'a'), (1, 'b'), (2, 'a'), (2, 'b').

multi-cartesian-product.title: How multi_cartesian_product() works
multi-cartesian-product.description: Every combination that takes one item from each of many lists.

note.text: one item from each list, in every possible way

slides.caption: multi_cartesian_product() works on an iterator of lists. Each result is a Vec with one item from every list.
Take 0 from list 1 and 0 from list 2: [0, 0].
The last list advances first: [0, 1].
List 2 is used up, so list 1 advances and list 2 starts again: [1, 0].
Then [1, 1]. Both lists are used up, so the iterator ends.
With n lists this is like n nested loops: these are the binary numbers 00, 01, 10, 11.

combinations.title: How combinations() works
combinations.description: Every way to choose k items, when order does not matter.

note.text: choose 2 of 3; [2, 1] is the same choice as [1, 2]

slides.caption: combinations(2) yields every way to choose 2 of the items, keeping them in their original order.
Start with the first two items: [1, 2].
Keep 1 and move the second choice on: [1, 3].
Move the first choice on to 2. Only 3 can follow it: [2, 3].
Choices like [2, 1] or [3, 1] are never made: they hold the same items as [1, 2] and [1, 3].
The result is [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3]. permutations(2) would also give the reversed orders: 6 in all.

combinations-with-replacement.title: How combinations_with_replacement() works
combinations-with-replacement.description: Like combinations(), but an item may be chosen more than once.

note.text: choose 2, and the same item may be picked again

slides.caption: combinations_with_replacement(2) puts each chosen item back, so it can be chosen again.
1 is chosen, put back, and chosen again: [1, 1].
Then 1 and 2: [1, 2].
2 twice: [2, 2]. [2, 1] is not given: it is the same choice as [1, 2].
Plain combinations(2) of [1, 2] would only give [1, 2]. With replacement there are 3 choices.

permutations.title: How permutations() works
permutations.description: Every ordered arrangement of k items: order matters.

slides.caption: permutations(2) yields every way to arrange 2 of the 3 items in a row.
1 first, then each of the others: [1, 2], [1, 3].
2 first: [2, 1], [2, 3]. [2, 1] counts, because the order is different from [1, 2].
3 choices for the first place × 2 for the second = 6. combinations(2) gives only 3.
All 6 arrangements, in order of the first item.

powerset.title: How powerset() works
powerset.description: Every subset of the items, from the empty one to all of them.

slides.caption: powerset() yields all combinations of size 0, then size 1, then size 2, and so on.
Size 0: the empty subset [].
Size 1: each item on its own.
Size 2: the combinations of 2 items.
Size 3: all the items. Each item is either in or out of a subset, so there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 subsets.
All 8 subsets. The number doubles with every extra item, so long inputs give huge results.

join.title: How join() works
join.description: Turns the items into one String with a separator between them.

note.text: the separator goes between items, not after the last

slides.caption: join() formats every item with Display and glues them into one String.
The first item starts the string: "1".
Before each later item, the separator ", " is added: "1, 2".
Then ", 3". There are no more items, so nothing is added after the 3.
join(", ") returns the String "1, 2, 3". An empty iterator gives an empty String.

intersperse.title: How intersperse() works
intersperse.description: Puts a separator item between every two items.

note.text: a 0 between items, never at the ends

slides.caption: intersperse(0) yields the items as they are, with a 0 between each pair of neighbours.
The first item, 1, comes out unchanged.
Before the next item a 0 is yielded, then 2.
Another 0, then 3.
The input is empty, so intersperse() stops. There is no 0 after the last item.
intersperse(0) yields 1, 0, 2, 0, 3. Use join() when you want a String instead.

merge.title: How merge() works
merge.description: Merges two sorted iterators into one sorted iterator.

note.text: both inputs are sorted, so the output is sorted too

slides.caption: merge() only ever looks at the front item of each input and yields the smaller one.
Compare the fronts: 1 and 2. 1 is smaller, so it comes out first.
Now 4 and 2: 2 is smaller.
4 and 3: 3 is smaller.
The first list is empty, so the rest of the second follows: 8.
Each item is compared once or twice, no sorting needed. If the inputs are not sorted, the output is not sorted either.

kmerge.title: How kmerge() works
kmerge.description: Merges any number of sorted iterators into one sorted iterator.

note.text: the smallest front item comes out each time

slides.caption: kmerge() keeps the front item of every list in a small heap and always yields the smallest.
Fronts: 1, 2, 3. The smallest is 1.
Fronts: 4, 2, 3. The smallest is 2.
Fronts: 4, 5, 3. The smallest is 3.
Fronts: 4, 5, 6. 4 comes out.
Then 5.
Only 6 is left.
Three sorted lists merged into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. With two lists, merge() does the same.

zip-longest.title: How zip_longest() works
zip-longest.description: Walks two iterators side by side and keeps going until both are empty.

slides.caption: zip_longest() yields an EitherOrBoth for each position: Both when both sides have an item, Left or Right when only one does.
Both sides have an item: Both(1, 'a').
The right side is empty. zip() would stop here; zip_longest() yields Left(2).
And Left(3). Then both sides are empty and it stops.
Every item appears once. Match on Both, Left and Right to handle each case.

interleave-shortest.title: How interleave_shortest() works
interleave-shortest.description: Takes turns between two iterators and stops when the one whose turn it is runs out.

note.text: stops as soon as a turn cannot be taken

slides.caption: interleave_shortest() takes one item from each side in turn, starting with the first.
First side: 1.
Second side: 2.
First side: 3. Second side: 4.
First side: 5.
It is the second side's turn, but it is empty, so the iterator stops. 7 is never yielded; interleave() would have yielded it.
The result is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Use interleave() to keep the rest of the longer side.

minmax.title: How minmax() works
minmax.description: Finds the smallest and the largest item in one pass.

note.text: both ends in one pass over the items

slides.caption: minmax() walks the items once and updates the smallest and largest seen so far.
The first item is both the smallest and the largest so far.
9 is larger than 4: the largest is now 9.
1 is smaller than 4: the smallest is now 1.
The items are used up. Calling min() and then max() would walk them twice.
The result is MinMax(1, 9). An empty iterator gives NoElements and a single item gives OneElement(x).

position-max.title: How position_max() works
position-max.description: Gives the index of the largest item, not the item itself.

slides.caption: position_max() remembers the largest item seen so far and its index.
Index 0 holds 4: the largest so far.
Index 1 holds 9, which is larger: remember index 1.
Index 2 holds 1, which is smaller: nothing changes.
The answer is the index, 1, wrapped in Some. When several items are equally large, the index of the last one is returned.
position_max() returns Some(1); an empty iterator gives None. max() would return Some(9) instead.

positions.title: How positions() works
positions.description: Gives the index of every item that matches a condition.

slides.caption: positions() tests every item and yields its index when the test is true.
Index 0 holds 1: odd, skipped.
Index 1 holds 2: even, so the index 1 is yielded.
Index 2 holds 3: odd, skipped.
Index 3 holds 4: even, so 3 is yielded.
The result is the indices 1, 3, not the items 2 and 4. Iterator::position() only finds the first match.

k-smallest.title: How k_smallest() works
k-smallest.description: Finds the k smallest items without sorting all of them.

note.text: only 2 items are kept at any time

slides.caption: k_smallest(2) keeps the 2 smallest items seen so far in a small heap. Anything larger is thrown away.
5 and 1 fill the 2 places.
4 is smaller than the largest kept item, 5, so 4 replaces 5.
2 is smaller than 4, so 2 replaces 4.
3 is larger than 2: it cannot be among the 2 smallest, so it is dropped.
At the end the kept items are sorted and yielded.
k_smallest(2) yields 1, 2. Memory use stays at k items, however long the input is.

sorted.title: How sorted() works
sorted.description: Collects any iterator and yields its items in sorted order.

slides.caption: sorted() cannot yield anything before it has seen every item: the smallest might be the last one.
First it collects all items into a Vec.
It sorts the Vec. 1 is smallest, so it comes out first.
Then 2.
Then 3.
sorted() yields 1, 2, 3 as an iterator, so you can keep chaining. The sort is stable: equal items keep their order.

sorted-by-key.title: How sorted_by_key() works
sorted-by-key.description: Sorts items by a key a function computes.

slides.caption: sorted_by_key() computes a key for every item and sorts by the keys.
The keys are the lengths: kiwi → 4, fig → 3, banana → 6.
The smallest key is 3: "fig" comes first.
Then key 4: "kiwi".
Then key 6: "banana".
Alphabetically the order would be banana, fig, kiwi. Items with equal keys keep their input order.

partition-map.title: How partition_map() works
partition-map.description: Splits items into two collections that can have different types.

note.text: Ok values go left, Err values go right

slides.caption: partition_map() calls a closure on each item. The closure returns Either::Left(v) or Either::Right(v), here: Ok(v) → Left(v), Err(e) → Right(e).
Ok(1) → Left(1): 1 goes into the left Vec<i32>.
Err("x") → Right("x"): "x" goes into the right Vec<&str>.
Ok(2) → Left(2).
The result is a tuple of two collections: ([1, 2], ["x"]). Iterator::partition() can only split into two collections of the same type.

coalesce.title: How coalesce() works
coalesce.description: Merges neighbouring items while a rule allows it.

note.text: merge (a, b) and (c, d) when c = b + 1

slides.caption: Each number becomes a range (x, x). coalesce() looks at the current range and the next one. The closure returns Ok(merged) to merge them, or Err to keep both.
The first range is (1, 1).
2 follows 1: merge into (1, 2).
3 follows 2: merge into (1, 3).
7 does not follow 3: (1, 3) is finished and yielded. (7, 7) starts.
8 follows 7: merge into (7, 8). The input ends, so (7, 8) is yielded.
Runs of consecutive numbers became ranges: (1, 3), (7, 8). The closure was |a, b| if a.1 + 1 == b.0 { Ok((a.0, b.1)) } else { Err((a, b)) }.

fold-while.title: How fold_while() works
fold-while.description: A fold that can stop before the end.

slides.caption: fold_while() works like fold(), but the closure returns Continue(acc) to go on or Done(acc) to stop. The closure: if acc + x <= 10 { Continue(acc + x) } else { Done(acc) }.
Start with acc = 0. 0 + 3 = 3 is ≤ 10: Continue(3).
3 + 4 = 7 is ≤ 10: Continue(7).
7 + 5 = 12 would be more than 10: Done(7). The fold stops here.
6 is never looked at.
fold_while() returns FoldWhile::Done(7); .into_inner() gives 7. A plain fold() cannot stop early.

tree-reduce.title: How tree_reduce() works
tree-reduce.description: Combines items pairwise, like a balanced tree, instead of left to right.

note.text: combine neighbours, then the results, and so on

slides.caption: tree_reduce() adds neighbours in pairs, then adds those results in pairs, until one value is left.
Second level: 3 + 7 = 10 and 11 + 15 = 26.
Third level: 10 + 26 = 36. Only one value is left.
fold() would compute ((((((1 + 2) + 3) + 4) + 5) + 6) + 7) + 8: 7 levels deep. The tree has 3 levels, which matters for floats and for combining strings or lists.
The sum is the same, 36, returned as Some(36). An empty iterator gives None. Before itertools 0.12 this method was called tree_fold1.

all-equal.title: How all_equal() works
all-equal.description: Checks whether every item is equal to the first one.

note.text: compare every item with the first

slides.caption: all_equal() takes the first item and compares every other item with it. It stops at the first difference.
[2, 2, 2]: every item equals the first, so the answer is true.
[2, 3]: 3 differs from 2, so the answer is false.
An empty iterator has no items that differ, so it gives true. A single item gives true as well.
Watch out for the empty case: all_equal() is true when there is nothing to compare. Use all_equal_value() to get the value too.

exactly-one.title: How exactly_one() works
exactly-one.description: Gets the only item, or an error when there are zero or several.

note.text: Ok only when there is exactly one item

slides.caption: exactly_one() reads at most two items: one to return and one more to check that there is nothing else.
[5]: one item and then the end: Ok(5).
An empty iterator: there is no item to return: Err.
[1, 2]: a second item exists: Err. The error still holds 1 and 2, so nothing is lost.
Use exactly_one() when more or fewer items would be a bug, for example a lookup that must match one row.
